text:
I run 25+ Grok Bots inside Codes Devs.

It looks like a small company in the sidebar.
Research. Ops. Publishing. Chief of Staff.

And the idea is catching fire: a post
recirculating a 10-to-20-Bot setup passed
five million views on X.

I get it. The market wants the roster.
Honestly, so do I.

But SpaceXAI own documentation says a
member’s Bots share one cloud computer:

Same files.
Same browser sessions.
Same sign-ins.
Same permissions.

That was the part I underestimated.

25 roles do not create 25 security
boundaries.

So my rule now is simple:
— one clear outcome per Bot
— minimum access
— approval before it sends, pays, or
publishes
— a receipt before I call anything done
— a human who owns the consequence

The org chart is fun.
The operating boundary is the actual
product.

I wrote up what I’m learning while running
this setup:
https://lnkd.in/dJvfXFJD

If you run Bots too: what broke first
access, approvals, evidence, or recovery?

Your agent might not need a better memory.

It might need to forget more. Word!

Building AgentSIM made this painfully clear.
A one-time code and a cleanup receipt can
belong to the same run, but giving them the
same lifetime would be mad!!

Agent memory isn’t just storage. It’s
deciding what deserves to survive, who can
trust it, and how it gets corrected or
deleted.

What’s your agent still holding onto that
should have disappeared already?

text:
YOUR AGENT GRAPH HAS AMNESIA.


While writing about graph engineering, I kept
coming back to one question:

What survives when the process restarts?

A workflow graph defines where work may go
next. It does not automatically preserve
which node ran, which artifact it used, why a
route fired, or what failed.

That belongs in a durable run record.

A knowledge graph is different. It connects
facts and entities, but a relationship is not
evidence. You still need to check the source.

I wrote the field guide I wanted while making
these decisions. It covers the parts box-
and-arrow diagrams tend to hide: state,
handoffs, recovery, verification, and human
authority.

The full field guide is in the first comment.
👇

Before adding another node, ask:

What does the graph make explicit that one
accountable loop cannot?

text:
Post 5
Text

getting a product to 70% is exciting.

getting from 70% to launch is where most
founders secretly lose their minds.

the first part feels like magic: you sketch
workflows, wire up agents, and see the core
loop function for the first time. you feel like
you’re flying.

then you hit the remaining stretch, and you
realize it is 90% unglamorous friction:

hunting down edge cases where an auth
token randomly expires.
rewriting user drop-off flows because
someone clicked back instead of forward.
staring at error logs at midnight trying to
understand why webhooks failed silently.
fixing broken state handling across basic
navigation.

none of this feels like building the future. it
feels like plumbing.

building Byro in tallinn at 19, this is the
biggest operational difference i’ve noticed
between talking about software and actually
shipping it.

anyone can build a demo that works in a
recorded video.

what separates real software from a
weekend prototype is having the patience to
fix the boring details nobody will ever
applaud you for.

Text 

we killed a profitable agency doing 4-figure
MRR to sit on the floor building software.

the reason wasn't that the agency was
failing. it was the delivery bottleneck:

every time we took on a new B2B client for
executive positioning, 80% of the work was
repetitive manual data plumbing:
- pulling signal from podcasts, sales calls, and
customer notes
- matching it to what target buyers were
actively talking about
- ghostwriting from scratch every single week

it worked, but it didn't scale past our own
calendar hours.

that's why we switched to building Byro as
software. 

if your service business relies on you manually
doing repetitive pattern matching, you don't
have an agency problem. you have a product
waiting to be built.

text:
Text

the best B2B marketing right now looks
closer to a high-end streetwear drop than
enterprise software.

when The Wall Street Journal wrote about
companies hiring storytellers for $270K+,
half of tech twitter laughed.

meanwhile teams like Clay took that exact
playbook and turned outbound into culture.

in the baltics and europe, we’re obsessed
with engineering depth. we build solid
architecture, optimize database queries, and
then write marketing copy that sounds like a
compliance manual.

consumer brands understand something
technical founders usually learn too late:
people do not buy feature checklists. they
buy taste, point of view, and the feeling
that the team behind the product actually
lives in the present.

when every startup has access to the exact
same llms and api wrappers, technical
execution becomes baseline table stakes.

the moat shifts to distribution, narrative,
and aesthetic standards.

if your product is technically brilliant but
nobody feels anything when they interact
with your brand, you’re competing purely on
price.

taste is what decides which tools become
defaults.

Text 

started uni in tallinn last week while trying
to get Byro from 70% to live.

the common advice for young founders is
binary: "drop out immediately or you aren't
serious."

that advice misses how modern building
actually works:
1. dev velocity with cursor and agentic
tooling means two people can build what used
to take a 6-person engineering team.
2. the bottleneck isn't typing code 14 hours
a day anymore. it's distribution, customer
discovery, and distribution loops.
3. campus gives you an immediate sandbox of
ambitious technical peers you can't replicate
sitting alone in a room.

the goal isn't playing the dramatic "college
dropout" founder role for optics. it's
ruthlessly protecting the 4-5 high-focus
hours every day where the product gets
built.
